title: Lecture 18. Evaluation of Prevention Effectiveness
summary:
1 Types of Internal Evaluation of Prevention Effectiveness

2 Types of External Evaluation of Prevention Effectiveness

In the USA in the 1960s, after the experience of the first wave of health prevention programs and the mixed results obtained, the question was raised: what should a prevention program be like and how should its results be evaluated? This gave rise to the development of a corresponding methodology.

This lesson provides a classification of approaches to evaluating the effectiveness of prevention programs. All methods can be divided into two types of program evaluation – internal and external. Internal evaluation relates to the properties of the program itself, while external evaluation relates to its results, i.e., how much and in what direction the behavior of its target groups has changed.

In this prevention project diagram, red highlights elements related only to external evaluation. All other elements of the diagram can be used for internal evaluation.

Methods of internal and external evaluation

1. Types of Internal Evaluation of Prevention Effectiveness

  • Adherence to the program's internal logic, adherence to its development procedure.

Example: If a program aims to reduce adolescent smoking by increasing awareness of the harms of smoking and developing refusal skills, the internal logic will be violated if most resources are directed towards sports activities not directly related to these goals.

  • Economic efficiency. Cost-benefit analysis: benefits are expressed in monetary terms (e.g., reduced costs for treating smoking-related diseases). Cost-effectiveness analysis: benefits are measured in non-monetary units (e.g., number of prevented disease cases, number of life-years saved). If a certain result can be achieved by different methods, preference is given to the least costly ones.

Cost-benefit analysis example: A flu vaccination program can be economically efficient if the costs of vaccination (vaccines, personnel) are lower than the economic losses from sick leave, reduced productivity, and treatment of flu complications.

Cost-effectiveness analysis example: Comparing two diabetes prevention programs: one based on individual counseling, the other on group sessions. Cost-effectiveness analysis can show which program provides a greater reduction in blood glucose levels per unit of expenditure.

  • Assessment of resource availability and quality: administrative, human, financial, material and technical, etc.
  • Monitoring the implementation of the prevention program plan: compliance of actual with planned deadlines, scope, and quality of work.
  • Expert analysis of program outcomes: a final analytical report, including a description of organizational difficulties and limitations of the completed project, an analysis of the reasons for achieving or not achieving program results, and recommendations for project development or scaling. Experts can be the program authors themselves, invited experts from various professional fields, and representatives of the program's target groups, or ideally, all three categories. For example, an expert group evaluating a school bullying prevention program might include psychologists, educators, social workers, and school administration representatives. Each expert will contribute their perspective on organizational aspects, psychological impact, and educational outcomes.
  • Selection of research design for external evaluation of the program, its short-term and long-term results.

2. Types of External Evaluation of Prevention Effectiveness The basis for external evaluation of a prevention project's outcomes is the "Expected Results" of the theoretical model. For each of these, appropriate indicators are selected to judge whether these results have been achieved. This is often not very easy to do. Not every expected result can have an unambiguous indicator. And not all of them can be easily verified. Sometimes this requires special studies, the cost of which may exceed the cost of the project itself.

Criteria for external program evaluation include changes in the behavior of its target group representatives, for example, an increase in those seeking professional help, a reduction in negative phenomena that the program aims to minimize — a decrease in the number of adolescent smokers, overweight students, or STI incidence.

Three main directions for evaluating project results can be identified:

a) comparisons with an ideal model, b) cross-sectional comparisons at interpersonal, intergroup, organizational, or territorial levels, c) temporal (longitudinal) evaluations of immediate and long-term changes. A) Comparisons with a given ideal model

  • Compliance with a given objective criterion for the target indicator of expected results. Often such criteria may be based on national standards, best international practices, or expert consensus, but may not always be realistic or applicable in a specific context. The closest example is the assessment of students' knowledge levels after completing a certain course. In prevention programs, the subject of evaluation may be changes in the awareness of a certain problem among target group representatives, for example, about HIV transmission routes, achieving a certain percentage of people who know their HIV status and are receiving treatment, in accordance with recommendations.
  • Assessment of subjective satisfaction with the quality and accessibility of services by target group representatives. Survey methods with scales for quantitative assessment or focus groups for obtaining more qualitative information can be used. For example, a survey of participants in a smoking cessation program can reveal how satisfied they are with the format of the sessions, the qualifications of the facilitators, the availability of materials and support, the quality of consultations received, etc.

B) Cross-sectional comparisons at interpersonal, intergroup, organizational, or territorial levels

  • Any diagnostic methods can be used within the framework of a cross-sectional or "case-control" study design. For example, surveying participants of a healthy eating program one month after its completion with the question: "How do you evaluate changes in your eating habits after participating in the program?"

C) Temporal (longitudinal) evaluations of immediate and long-term changes

  • Long-term socio-statistical comparisons of dynamic data series across territories or organizations. For example, tracking the dynamics of HIV incidence in a region before, during, and after the implementation of a large-scale prevention program. Or comparing the dynamics of various types of adolescent deviance in city districts where a prevention program is being conducted versus where it is not.
  • "Before-After" evaluation within the framework of a retrospective cohort study design. For example, conducting a series (more than one) of surveys among schoolchildren in schools where a long-term bullying prevention program is implemented, and in control schools where such a program is absent, using identical questions about bullying experience and awareness of the problem.
  • Prospective cohort study with a control group and randomization — the most evidence-based method for evaluating effectiveness.

Example: A randomized controlled trial (RCT) of the effectiveness of a new depression prevention program among adolescents. One group of adolescents receives the program, the other does not (or receives standard treatment). Depression levels are assessed before the program begins and at specific intervals after its completion. Comparing the dynamics of indicators in both groups allows for a reliable judgment of the program's effectiveness.

The choice of evaluation method depends on the program's goals, available resources, and ethical considerations. There is no universal "best" method; its selection is determined by the circumstances in which the program is implemented. Significant advantages in program evaluation include:

combining various evaluation methods and comparing their results, involving representatives of the program's target groups in the evaluation, critical reflection on evaluation results, with the aim not just to show a result, but to initiate a constructive dialogue with representatives of the professional community.
